title: Tea for Whoever Returns
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The first cup after the repair was terrible.

Iroh knew before he tasted it.

Mina had set the kettle too close to the new stove vent, and the water heated faster than expected. The leaves steeped too long while everyone admired the fact that the second kitchen was finally dry.

He took one sip and made a face.

I nearly laughed tea through my nose.

"Well?" I asked.

"Powerful," he said.

"That bad?"

"One might mistake it for a declaration of war."

Mina groaned.

Iroh put down the cup.

"Then let's make another."

The repaired kitchen was smaller than the plans had promised, but safer. The backflow device had been tested under the next storm conditions. Tamsin had signed off on the new drainage channel. Bo had helped revise the cleaning checklist, and the staff had been paid for the extra days spent moving supplies.

A new sign beside the back door explained what the warning sounds meant and whom to contact if the drain began to gurgle.

It wasn't a beautiful sign.

It might save the shop.

The public room was ready too. We had moved the tables to keep a clear path from the entrance to the garden, and Edda had tested the turn around the window seat. The little table Halen sometimes chose was still near the back. The front table stood unreserved.

That decision had caused a small argument.

"Surely," Mara said, "you want to keep one seat for your regulars?"

Iroh shook his head.

"Regulars have favorite places. They do not own them."

"Then what if someone comes back and finds their chair occupied?"

"Then we offer another chair."

Mara considered.

"Fair."

I thought of all the ways people tried to turn belonging into a reserved place, a promise that no one else could sit where they had sat before.

The teahouse had room for people to return without keeping everyone else waiting.

We opened at noon.

The first customer was a child with a very muddy boot. The second was Halen, who inspected the new floor and informed us that the old boards had been less slippery.

"That's because they were cracked," I said.

"Cracks can be useful," he replied.

Iroh offered him tea.

He accepted, but chose a different table from his usual one.

A little later, Danse came in with Toph to discuss the shared drainage report. They argued about a measurement near the canal and then, astonishingly, agreed on the next test. Greg arrived carrying a small stack of chairs for the upcoming public meeting. Maui helped bring them inside without announcing his heroic arrival.

I watched the room fill with the people whose work had made the reopening possible.

Not an audience.

A community.

At the counter, Iroh was pouring the affordable house blend. He had kept its price steady through the repair, with the costs recorded openly in the ledger. The growers were still facing a difficult season, and the clinic still needed a reserved supply of mountain mint.

We hadn't solved scarcity by wishing.

We'd changed how we shared it.

In the late afternoon, a traveler arrived through the Jasmine Door carrying a small bag and looking uncertain. They stood just inside the entrance, watching the room.

Iroh approached gently.

"Welcome. Would you like a table?"

The traveler glanced toward the empty one by the window.

"Is that reserved?"

"No."

"Do I need to tell you how long I'm staying?"

"Only if you wish to make an arrangement."

They smiled, relieved.

"I'd like tea."

"Then tea it is."

He seated them without asking for a story.

I watched from behind the counter, feeling something settle inside me.

A second customer came in just before closing, carrying a small parcel from a neighboring stall. The paper had been wrapped in string and tied so badly that the whole package looked ready to fall apart.

"I heard the kitchen reopened," they said. "My mother wanted you to have this."

Inside was a little clay cup, mismatched with every cup in the shop. Iroh held it carefully.

"Why?"

"Because she used to stop here after market day. She said you gave her tea when she was tired."

He looked touched, then uncomfortable. "We can't accept a gift every time we sell a cup."

"You don't have to display it. She just wanted you to know she remembered."

We thanked them. After they left, Iroh put the clay cup on the shelf with the shop's other mismatched pieces rather than giving it a place of honor that would make the customer feel indebted next time.

"The valley taught me a great many things," he said. "I am trying to bring the useful ones home."

"This is already your home," I told him.

He smiled. The Jasmine Dragon was a real Ba Sing Se business, with workers who needed wages, growers who deserved fair prices and customers whose kindness didn't erase a debt. The Lanternweald had its own Jasmine Steps, and its own stories. I loved visiting both without confusing them.

Iroh took my hand across the account book. "Would you like to stay a while?"

"Yes. I have other plans later in the week, and I know you do too. Tonight I'd like to be here."

He nodded. We had learned to speak about ethical non-monogamy and my preference for polyamory in ordinary sentences, not just at moments when one of us feared being left behind.

"Then let us finish the accounts," he said, "and make the next cup properly."

I laughed. The shop needed no grand ending to stay alive after a story finished. It needed a kettle, people who chose to come in, and people willing to open the door again tomorrow.

After closing, we counted the till. It wasn't an impressive sum. The repair debt remained, and the next delivery would still cost more than we'd hoped.

Iroh checked the figures and closed the ledger.

"Enough for the next step," he said.

I looked at him.

"You're learning to sound like Greg."

"Then perhaps I shall acquire a guitar."

"Please don't."

He laughed.

We carried the cups into the second kitchen. The walls smelled faintly of fresh plaster, and the window had been repaired so it no longer rattled when the wind changed.

Iroh set a kettle on the stove.

"Would you like tea?" he asked.

"Only if you're making it."

"An alarming amount of trust."

"You've earned it."

He smiled.

The tea was good this time, warm and gently bitter, with the citrus at the end just as it should be.

We drank in silence for a while.

Then he took my hand.

"Are you happy?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Even when the roof leaks and the drain floods and your life is full of complicated people?"

"Especially then, sometimes. Not because the problems are good. Because we can face them honestly."

He looked thoughtful.

"I once believed peace was a place one reached after every battle had ended."

"And now?"

"Now I think it is sometimes a cup of tea while tomorrow remains uncertain."

I set down my cup and moved closer.

"May I kiss you?"

He smiled.

"I was hoping you would."

His lips met mine, warm and patient. He held my hand against his chest, and I felt the quiet rhythm of his heartbeat. We kissed again, slower this time, with no need to make the moment a declaration against any of my other relationships.

I loved him. That was enough.

Later we went upstairs, leaving the last clean cups to dry. The evening stayed private, full of soft laughter and the ordinary comfort of being wanted without being owned.

At dawn, I woke to the smell of tea.

Iroh stood by the window with two cups and a look of tremendous satisfaction.

"You're up early," I said.

"The kettle is punctual."

"Unlike the roof."

"An unfortunate comparison."

I took a cup.

Outside, the streets of Ba Sing Se glittered with rainwater that was flowing the proper direction. People were opening shops, sweeping paths, carrying bread, and deciding where to go next.

The table by the window remained unreserved.

We would make tea for whoever chose to return.

And when the day was done, we would still be allowed to choose one another.
